title: Where Names Live
content:
What problem does this solve?
A function call gets its own local names. Parameters are local names created from the caller's arguments. A variable assigned inside a function normally belongs to that function call, so the same spelling inside and outside does not automatically mean the same stored value.

Same spelling, different place
  name = "outside"
  def show():
      name = "inside"
      print(name)
  show()
  print(name)
The function prints inside; the outer name still stores outside.

Prefer explicit dependencies
When a helper needs information, pass it in as a parameter. When it produces information, return it. That is easier to reason about and test than secretly depending on outside state.

Read before local assignment
If a function assigns to a name, Python normally treats that name as local in the function. Trying to read that local value before it has been assigned produces UnboundLocalError.

Vocabulary after the behavior
Scope describes where a name is available. A local variable belongs to one function call. Shadowing means a local name uses the same spelling as an outside name without replacing it.
concepts: Parameters and variables assigned inside a function are local to that call
A local name can have the same spelling as an outside name without changing it
Passing dependencies as parameters makes functions easier to reason about and test
return carries a local result back to the caller
Assigning to a name inside a function makes a read-before-assignment of that local name fail

examples.title: Inside then outside
examples.code:
name = "outside"
def show():
    name = "inside"
    print(name)
show()
print(name)
examples.explanation: The local assignment does not replace the outer value.

examples.title: Parameter instead of hidden state
examples.code:
rate = 2
def total(amount, rate):
    return amount * rate
print(total(5, 3))
examples.explanation: The helper receives the rate it needs explicitly instead of secretly reading the outer rate.

examples.title: Read before assignment
examples.explanation: Because the function assigns to count, count is local there; the right side would read it before a local value exists.

common_mistakes: Assuming assignment inside a function automatically changes a same-named outside variable
Using globals because passing a parameter feels repetitive
Reading a would-be local before assigning it
Turning “avoid hidden globals” into a slogan instead of understanding explicit dependencies

exercises.title: Inside then outside
exercises.prompt: Write the exact two output lines.
exercises.code_to_predict:
name = "outside"
def show():
    name = "inside"
    print(name)
show()
print(name)
hints: Trace the function call separately from the outer code.
Inside show, the local name stores inside. After the call, the outer name still stores outside.
The lines are inside, then outside.

exercises.title: The outside value stays
exercises.code_to_predict:
status = "waiting"
def prepare():
    status = "ready"
    return status
prepare()
print(status)
hints: prepare returns ready, but the caller does not store that returned value.
The assignment inside prepare is local to the function call.
The outside status remains waiting.

exercises.title: Make the dependency explicit
exercises.prompt: Rewrite `double_total` so it receives `total` as a parameter instead of reading the outside variable. Keep the outer total equal to 5 and print the result of `double_total(7)`, which should be 14.
exercises.starter_code:
total = 5

def double_total():
    return total * 2

print(double_total())
exercises.reference_solution:
total = 5

def double_total(total):
    return total * 2

print(double_total(7))
hints: Put total inside the function parameter list so each call supplies the value explicitly.
Use only the parameter inside the function body; then call it with 7.
Define `double_total(total)` returning `total * 2`, then print `double_total(7)`.

exercises.title: Which helper is easier to test?
exercises.prompt: Which design makes the function's dependency clearest and easiest to test?
choices: A function silently reads and changes an outside `supplies` variable.
A function receives `supplies` as a parameter and returns its result.
hints: Ask whether a caller can see all inputs from the function call itself.
Hidden outside state makes behavior depend on information not shown in the call.
Choose the explicit parameter/return design.

exercises.title: Why does this fail?
exercises.prompt:
What best explains the problem in this function?

count = 3
def use_one():
    count = count - 1
    return count
choices: The assignment makes count local, so the right side tries to read that local before it has a value.
Python automatically changes the global count first.
Subtraction is not allowed inside a function.
hints: Notice that count is assigned inside the function.
That assignment makes count a local name for this function body unless special syntax is used.
The right side reads the local count before any local value has been assigned, causing UnboundLocalError.

exercises.title: Repair the hidden dependency
exercises.prompt: Refactor this function to receive supplies as a parameter and return one less. Print `use_supply(supplies)`. The outside `supplies` variable must remain 3.
exercises.starter_code:
supplies = 3
def use_supply():
    supplies = supplies - 1
    return supplies
print(use_supply())
exercises.reference_solution:
supplies = 3
def use_supply(supplies):
    supplies = supplies - 1
    return supplies
print(use_supply(supplies))
hints: Turn the value the function needs into a parameter.
The local parameter can be reassigned without changing the outside integer variable.
Define `use_supply(supplies)`, subtract 1 locally, return it, and call `use_supply(supplies)`.

exercises.title: Apply damage explicitly
exercises.prompt: Write `apply_damage(health, hit)` that returns `health - hit` and reads no outside variables.
exercises.reference_solution:
def apply_damage(health, hit):
    return health - hit
hints: Both pieces of information belong in the function call.
Use the two parameter names directly in the arithmetic expression.
Return `health - hit`.

exercises.title: Keep both inputs local
exercises.prompt: Write `format_pair(first, second)` returning `<first> | <second>`. Use only its parameters/local names; do not read any outside variable.
hints: The returned text is built entirely from the two arguments for this call.
Use an f-string with first and second.
Return `f"{first} | {second}"`.

exercises.title: Local Party Report
exercises.prompt: Keep the supplied outside `total_health = 999`. Write `party_report(party)` for a non-empty list of member dictionaries. Using only the parameter and local names, return a dictionary with `member_count`, `total_health`, and `lowest_health`. Sum all health values and track the lowest health without using `min()`. The outside total_health must remain 999.
hints: Start both local calculations inside the function: total at 0 and lowest health from the guaranteed first member.
Visit every member. Add health to the local total and replace lowest_health only when the current health is smaller.
Return the three named fields after the loop. Do not assign to the outside variable; the local name may have the same spelling safely.
exercises.success_message: The report is fully determined by its argument and local state; a second party produces a second independent result.
